`/var/log/myapp` is not readable from this session, so I checked the script itself.

## What happened

The `unlink` call at line 23 could not delete `/var/log/myapp/app.log`.

Errno 13 is `EACCES`. On Linux, `unlink` checks the permission bits of the parent directory. It does not check the permission bits of the file. So the message points at `/var/log/myapp`, not at `app.log`. Your account can read the file, because the copy on line 21 succeeded. Your account cannot delete an entry from that directory.

## Check the directory before you run the script again

Line 23 runs after the `with` block on lines 21-22 closes. The copy therefore finished. `/var/log/myapp/app.log.gz` now exists and holds a complete copy. `/var/log/myapp/app.log` also still exists. Both files are on disk.

Two effects follow:

1. A second run compresses `app.log` again, overwrites `app.log.gz`, and fails at the same line. The script makes no progress.
2. The exception leaves the loop at line 41. Any log file sorted after `app.log` never rotates, and `prune_archives` never runs.

## One detail does not fit

Line 21 creates `app.log.gz` in that same directory. A new file needs the same directory write permission that `unlink` needs. That create did not fail. Two explanations fit:

- `app.log.gz` already existed and your account owns it. Then `gzip.open` needed write permission on that file only.
- A mandatory access control module (SELinux or AppArmor) permits the write and denies the delete. Both return `EACCES`.

Run these to tell the two apart:

```
ls -la /var/log/myapp/
stat -c '%U %G %a' /var/log/myapp /var/log/myapp/app.log
id
sudo journalctl -k --since -1h | grep -iE 'avc|apparmor'
```

## How to fix the permission

Pick one:

- Run the rotation as the owner of `/var/log/myapp`. This is usually `root` or the service account.
- Add your account to the directory's group. Then set the group write bit on the directory.

Do not widen the permissions on `/var/log` itself.

## A larger problem sits behind this one

A running service probably holds `app.log` open. A delete does not free the disk space in that case. The service keeps its file descriptor and writes to an inode with no name. You lose those lines, and the space returns only at the next service restart.

Two standard answers exist:

- Copy the file, then truncate the original to zero length. `logrotate` calls this `copytruncate`.
- Send the service a signal to reopen its log. Many daemons use `SIGHUP`.

`logrotate` solves this and the permission problem. Consider it before you invest more work in the script.

## Other defects in the script

1. `compress` overwrites an existing archive (line 20). Two rotations of `app.log` produce the same target name, so the second destroys the first archive. Add a timestamp to the target name.
2. `compress` is not atomic (lines 21-23). A crash mid-copy leaves a truncated `.gz`. Write to a temporary name, then rename it.
3. `rotate` stops at the first failure (line 41). One bad file blocks every later file. Catch the error per file, continue, then exit non-zero with a report.
4. A failed `unlink` leaves the new `.gz` in place. Delete that archive on failure, or the directory collects duplicates.
5. `prune_archives` globs `*.gz` (line 28). It deletes archives that `--pattern` does not cover. Scope the glob to the pattern.
6. `--keep 0` deletes nothing (line 29). `archives[:-0]` is an empty list. Guard `keep` at zero.

Tell me if you want me to apply items 1 through 6 to `fixture/rotate_logs.py`.
